title: Preeclampsia: Severe Features Mean Escalate
bottomLine: Preeclampsia can worsen rapidly and can occur postpartum. Severe-range blood pressure or symptoms such as persistent severe headache, visual disturbance, RUQ/epigastric pain, dyspnea, neurologic change, or seizure require immediate obstetric escalation.
recognize: Hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or end-organ features may indicate preeclampsia.
Severe features can include severe hypertension, thrombocytopenia, liver injury, renal dysfunction, pulmonary edema, or persistent neurologic symptoms.
Postpartum preeclampsia may occur after discharge.
priorities: Assess blood pressure correctly and repeat severe values promptly per protocol.
Assess headache, vision, RUQ/epigastric pain, respiratory status, reflexes/clonus when relevant, and fetal status if pregnant.
Initiate seizure precautions and escalate severe features immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, urine output, platelets, creatinine, liver enzymes, symptoms, and fetal monitoring as ordered.
During magnesium therapy, monitor respirations, reflexes, urine output, and signs of toxicity.
interventions: Administer prescribed antihypertensives and magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis/treatment when indicated.
Maintain a quiet environment and prepare for urgent delivery planning when clinically indicated.
medicationSafety: Magnesium toxicity can cause loss of reflexes, respiratory depression, and cardiac arrest; calcium gluconate is the antidote used for significant toxicity.
Low urine output increases magnesium accumulation risk.
teaching: Teach postpartum warning signs and the need for urgent evaluation even after delivery.
Reinforce BP follow-up and medication adherence when prescribed.
delegationScope: Routine stable-patient vital signs may be delegated with explicit reporting thresholds, but severe BP or new neurologic/respiratory symptoms require immediate licensed-nurse assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Assuming delivery cures preeclampsia immediately and dismissing a postpartum severe headache.
oneLinePearl: Preeclampsia does not end at delivery—postpartum danger is real.
sourceBasis: ACOG Practice Bulletin: Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia

title: Postpartum Hemorrhage: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin
bottomLine: Postpartum hemorrhage is an emergency in which visible blood loss may underestimate severity. Assess uterine tone, bleeding, vital signs, and perfusion immediately while activating the obstetric hemorrhage response.
recognize: A boggy enlarged uterus suggests uterine atony, the most common cause.
A firm uterus with ongoing heavy bleeding raises concern for laceration or retained tissue/other causes.
Tachycardia, pallor, dizziness, altered mentation, or hypotension indicate worsening blood loss.
priorities: Call for help/activate hemorrhage protocol.
Assess fundal tone and lochia/bleeding while checking vital signs and perfusion.
Massage a boggy uterus and empty the bladder as ordered/appropriate.
Administer uterotonics and fluids/blood products per protocol.
assessMonitor: Quantify blood loss when possible, trend vital signs, urine output, mental status, uterine tone, and response to therapy.
interventions: Maintain large-bore IV access per acute-care protocol.
Prepare for additional uterotonics, tranexamic acid, procedures, or surgery if bleeding persists.
medicationSafety: Methylergonovine is generally avoided in hypertension/preeclampsia.
Carboprost is generally avoided in asthma because of bronchospasm risk.
teaching: After stabilization, teach warning signs of delayed postpartum hemorrhage and when to seek urgent care.
delegationScope: This is an emergency; the PN initiates immediate measures within scope and remains engaged while escalating to the RN/obstetric team.
examTrap: Waiting for hypotension before treating heavy postpartum bleeding.
oneLinePearl: Boggy uterus: massage and escalate; firm uterus plus bleeding: think beyond atony.
sourceBasis: Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health Obstetric Hemorrhage Bundle

title: Magnesium Sulfate: Prevent Seizures, Watch Respirations
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Magnesium sulfate is used for seizure prophylaxis/treatment in preeclampsia/eclampsia, not primarily to lower blood pressure. Respiratory depression, absent reflexes, and reduced urine output are major toxicity warnings.
recognize: Expected effects can include warmth, flushing, nausea, and lethargy.
Toxicity risk increases when renal clearance is reduced.
priorities: Assess respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes, level of consciousness, and urine output before and during therapy.
Stop the infusion and escalate immediately for toxicity signs per protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory status, reflexes, urine output, BP, and serum magnesium when ordered/clinically indicated.
interventions: Keep calcium gluconate available according to obstetric protocol.
medicationSafety: Magnesium can cause respiratory and neuromuscular depression at toxic levels.
Antihypertensive therapy is still needed for severe hypertension when indicated because magnesium is not the BP treatment.
complications: Neonatal respiratory depression with significant exposure
teaching: Explain that the medication prevents seizures and that close monitoring is expected.
delegationScope: Infusion management authority varies by state/facility for LPN/LVN practice; follow policy and escalate toxicity signs immediately.
examTrap: Assuming magnesium sulfate is working because the blood pressure decreased slightly.
oneLinePearl: Magnesium protects the brain; respirations and reflexes protect the patient.

title: Pediatric Dehydration: Perfusion Before the Percent
bottomLine: Children can compensate until dehydration becomes advanced. Tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, reduced urine output, dry mucosa, absent tears, lethargy, and poor intake are more important than one isolated sign.
recognize: Infants may show fewer wet diapers, sunken fontanelle, poor feeding, and irritability or lethargy.
Weight change is a useful objective measure when reliable baseline weight is available.
Hypotension is a late sign in pediatric shock.
priorities: Assess mental status, heart rate, capillary refill, mucous membranes, tears, urine output, and ability to drink.
Use oral rehydration for mild/moderate dehydration when safe; severe dehydration or shock needs urgent IV/IO resuscitation.
assessMonitor: Trend weight, intake/output, urine output, heart rate, capillary refill, electrolytes when indicated, and response to rehydration.
interventions: Give small frequent amounts of oral rehydration solution rather than plain water or sugary drinks.
medicationSafety: Avoid antidiarrheal medications in young children unless specifically ordered and appropriate.
Rapid correction of certain electrolyte disorders requires clinician-directed protocols.
teaching: Teach oral rehydration solution use, continued feeding, wet-diaper monitoring, and return precautions.
delegationScope: Intake/output and diaper counts may be delegated with clear reporting parameters; assessment of worsening perfusion requires licensed-nurse evaluation.
examTrap: Using plain water alone to replace losses in an infant with significant gastroenteritis.
oneLinePearl: Kids lose pressure late—watch perfusion and urine output early.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Pediatrics Oral Rehydration Guidance

title: Croup vs Epiglottitis: Do Not Agitate the Airway
bottomLine: Barking cough and inspiratory stridor suggest croup; drooling, tripod positioning, muffled voice, toxic appearance, and severe distress raise concern for epiglottitis or another critical upper-airway obstruction. Do not force a throat examination in a child with suspected epiglottitis.
recognize: Croup often includes barking cough, hoarseness, and stridor, frequently after viral symptoms.
Epiglottitis may present with abrupt fever, severe sore throat, drooling, tripod posture, dysphagia, and muffled voice.
priorities: Keep the child calm and with caregiver when possible.
Assess airway effort, stridor at rest, oxygenation, color, and mental status.
For suspected epiglottitis, avoid throat manipulation and prepare for controlled airway management.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory effort, stridor, oxygenation, retractions, and fatigue.
interventions: Give dexamethasone for croup and nebulized epinephrine for moderate/severe croup when ordered.
Provide oxygen if hypoxemic while minimizing agitation.
medicationSafety: Nebulized epinephrine can improve symptoms temporarily; recurrence can occur, so observation is required after treatment.
teaching: Teach caregivers when stridor at rest, retractions, cyanosis, poor intake, or lethargy require urgent care.
delegationScope: Acute upper-airway symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment; do not delegate evaluation of stridor or drooling.
examTrap: Using a tongue depressor to inspect the throat of a drooling child sitting forward in severe distress.
oneLinePearl: Drool plus tripod: hands off the throat, call airway help.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Pediatrics Upper Airway Infection Guidance

title: Febrile Seizure: Protect, Time, Reassure Appropriately
bottomLine: A simple febrile seizure is brief, generalized, and occurs once in 24 hours in the typical age range, but prolonged, focal, recurrent, or atypical events require further evaluation. During the seizure, use standard seizure safety—no objects in the mouth.
recognize: Simple febrile seizures commonly occur from about 6 months to 5 years of age.
The fever itself is usually caused by an infection; the seizure does not automatically mean meningitis.
priorities: Protect from injury, place side-lying when possible, time the seizure, and monitor breathing.
Afterward assess neurologic recovery and the cause/source of fever.
Escalate prolonged, focal, recurrent, or atypical seizures.
assessMonitor: Assess duration, focality, recurrence, immunization history, neck stiffness, petechiae, persistent altered mental status, and hydration.
interventions: Treat discomfort from fever with age-appropriate antipyretics as ordered; antipyretics do not reliably prevent recurrence.
medicationSafety: Avoid aspirin in children with viral illness because of Reye syndrome risk.
Rescue benzodiazepines may be ordered for prolonged seizures and require respiratory monitoring.
complications: Underlying CNS infection in selected presentations
teaching: Teach seizure first aid, recurrence risk, fever comfort measures, and when to call EMS.
delegationScope: Any staff can initiate basic seizure safety; licensed-nurse assessment is needed for atypical features and postictal recovery.
examTrap: Telling parents that scheduled antipyretics will prevent future febrile seizures.
oneLinePearl: Febrile seizure care is seizure safety first, fever cause second.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Pediatrics Febrile Seizure Guidance

title: Suicide Risk: Ask Directly and Protect Immediately
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Directly asking about suicidal thoughts does not create suicidal intent. If a patient has current intent, a plan, access to lethal means, escalating behavior, or cannot maintain safety, do not leave the patient alone and initiate the emergency safety pathway.
recognize: Warning signs include hopelessness, feeling trapped or burdensome, giving away possessions, abrupt mood change, increased substance use, agitation, or recent major loss.
A sudden calm after severe depression can be concerning if it reflects a decision to attempt suicide.
priorities: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plan, intent, timing, prior attempts, and access to means.
Maintain observation/safety precautions proportional to risk.
Remove hazards per policy and escalate to the mental-health/emergency team.
assessMonitor: Reassess risk after changes in mood, medication, privileges, visitors, or disposition.
Document exact statements and observed behavior rather than vague labels.
interventions: Use calm, nonjudgmental communication and collaborative safety planning when appropriate.
Do not rely on a no-suicide contract as a safety intervention.
medicationSafety: Monitor for activation, agitation, or worsening suicidal thinking after starting/changing antidepressant therapy, especially in younger patients, and report concerning changes promptly.
teaching: Teach the patient/family how to reduce access to lethal means and how to access crisis/emergency services as part of the clinical plan.
delegationScope: Observation may be assigned according to policy, but suicide-risk assessment and changes in precautions require licensed clinical judgment and team escalation.
examTrap: Avoiding the word suicide because asking directly might put the idea in the patient's head.
oneLinePearl: Ask clearly, stay with high risk, remove means, escalate.
sourceBasis: The Joint Commission Suicide Prevention Resources
SAMHSA Suicide Risk and Safety Planning Guidance

title: Alcohol Withdrawal: Seizure and Delirium Risk
bottomLine: Alcohol withdrawal can progress from tremor and autonomic symptoms to seizures and delirium tremens. A history of heavy use plus abrupt reduction warrants structured assessment, seizure precautions, and timely medication treatment when indicated.
recognize: Early findings include tremor, anxiety, diaphoresis, nausea, insomnia, tachycardia, and hypertension.
Seizures and delirium can occur with severe withdrawal.
Older adults and medically ill patients can deteriorate quickly.
priorities: Assess timing/amount of last alcohol use, prior withdrawal seizures/DTs, vital signs, mental status, hydration, and co-occurring illness.
Use the facility withdrawal scale/protocol when appropriate.
Initiate seizure/fall precautions and give benzodiazepines as ordered for clinically significant withdrawal.
assessMonitor: Trend withdrawal score, vital signs, orientation, hallucinations, fluid/electrolyte status, and response to medication.
interventions: Provide thiamine as ordered, especially before or with glucose in patients at risk for deficiency, without delaying urgent treatment of hypoglycemia.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines can cause oversedation and respiratory depression.
Do not give alcohol as a routine treatment for withdrawal.
teaching: After stabilization, connect the patient with evidence-based treatment for alcohol use disorder and relapse-prevention resources.
delegationScope: Routine observation and vitals may be delegated with exact thresholds; interpretation of withdrawal progression and medication response requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming a sleeping patient after repeated benzodiazepines is simply improving without checking respiratory status and sedation depth.
oneLinePearl: Withdrawal can kill; treat the autonomic storm and watch the airway.
sourceBasis: ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management

title: Acute Mania: Safety, Sleep, Nutrition, Boundaries
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Acute mania can impair judgment, sleep, nutrition, and safety. Use calm firm limits, reduce stimulation, offer portable high-calorie foods/fluids, protect sleep, and monitor for escalating agitation, psychosis, or dangerous behavior.
recognize: Elevated or irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, grandiosity, impulsivity, and increased goal-directed activity are classic clues.
Severe mania may include psychosis, aggression, or profound exhaustion/dehydration.
priorities: Assess immediate risk to self/others, psychosis, substance use, sleep deprivation, hydration, and nutrition.
Set brief consistent limits on unsafe behavior.
Reduce environmental stimulation and structure activities.
assessMonitor: Track sleep, intake, hydration, activity, impulsivity, medication adherence, and escalating agitation.
interventions: Offer finger foods and fluids if the patient cannot sit for meals.
Use simple concrete communication and avoid power struggles.
medicationSafety: Lithium requires monitoring for toxicity and renal/thyroid effects; dehydration and sodium depletion can increase lithium levels.
Antipsychotics can cause sedation, orthostasis, metabolic effects, and extrapyramidal symptoms.
teaching: After stabilization, reinforce medication adherence, sleep routine, substance avoidance, and early warning signs of relapse.
delegationScope: Structured activities and observation may be assigned per policy, but behavioral assessment and medication-effect evaluation require licensed-nurse judgment.
examTrap: Trying to challenge grandiose beliefs through prolonged logical debate during acute mania.
oneLinePearl: Mania care is structure without confrontation.
sourceBasis: American Psychiatric Association Bipolar Disorder Guidance

title: Lithium: Hydration, Sodium, and Toxicity
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index. Dehydration, sodium depletion, kidney dysfunction, and interacting medications can raise levels; new coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, vomiting/diarrhea, or marked drowsiness should trigger holding the drug and urgent evaluation per protocol.
recognize: Fine tremor, mild thirst, and increased urination may occur at therapeutic doses; worsening neurologic or GI findings suggest toxicity.
Older adults and patients with kidney disease are at greater risk.
priorities: Assess neurologic status, hydration, GI losses, renal function, sodium intake changes, and interacting medications.
Hold and report suspected toxicity according to order/policy.
Obtain serum lithium level and renal/electrolyte testing when ordered.
assessMonitor: Trend lithium levels, renal function, thyroid function, sodium, fluid status, and medication interactions.
interventions: Maintain consistent fluid and sodium intake unless otherwise medically directed.
Escalate severe toxicity for emergency management; dialysis may be required in selected cases.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and thiazide diuretics can increase lithium concentrations.
Dehydration from vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or heavy sweating can increase toxicity risk.
teaching: Teach consistent salt/fluid intake, avoiding unapproved NSAIDs, keeping lab appointments, and calling before continuing lithium during significant dehydration illness.
delegationScope: Medication administration is within licensed scope as permitted; suspected toxicity requires prompt licensed-nurse assessment and prescriber/RN escalation.
examTrap: Telling a patient on lithium to follow a low-sodium diet to reduce blood pressure without coordinating the medication plan.
oneLinePearl: Lithium hates dehydration and sudden sodium changes.
